Business tort law involves the legal ramifications of engaging in business or commerce, whether directly with clients or in connection with other businesses. There are myriad aspects of business tort law, and business owners should be familiar with the issues that can result in liability.
Although the terms are often used interchangeably, a business tort is not the same as a business crime. Business crimes, also known as white collar crimes, involve illegal activities in furtherance of a business or with a business purpose. White collar crimes can include fraud, money laundering, bribery, forgery, and embezzlement. Business torts are not criminal activities, but do involve civil liability.
Business tort liability can arise in relation to a variety of business functions, including, but not limited to, sales, marketing, advertising, and employment. For example, a company might be held liable in connection with:
- a sales representative who makes false representations about a product,
- an employer who infringes on an employee’s patent,
- a manufacturer who fails to pay royalties to a licensing agency,
- a company that posts false information about its competitors, and
- a company that engages in tortious interference with a business relationship.
Business torts are distinguished from other types of torts in that there need not be any contractual relationship between the parties. For example, a store owner who fails to clean a spill after being warned, a delivery driver who causes a crash, a website that publishes a false accusation, or a manufacturer whose product injures a bystander can all face liability without any contract.

- Torts in connection with employment – This type of business tort involves the failure of an employer to provide safe working conditions for its employees.
- Unintentional torts – This type of business tort involves the unintentional causing of harm to another person or property.
- Intentional torts – This type of business tort involves the intentional causing of harm to another person or property.
- Torts in connection with contracts – This type of business tort involves the failure of a party to a contract to perform its obligations under the contract.

The Texas Legislature created the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force in 2013 to try to figure out why the state has one of the highest rates of women dying from pregnancy-related causes in the country. The task force has brought together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and public health experts to review individual maternal deaths case by case. The task force uncovered huge gaps in data collection and a troubling racial disparity, reporting that Black women in Texas are dying from pregnancy-related causes at far higher rates than white or Hispanic women.
In the task force's early analysis, Black women accounted for about one in nine births in Texas but nearly three in ten maternal deaths. Later reviews found that errors that included problems with how pregnancy was recorded on death certificates had inflated some of those figures, but the analysis still showed that Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at much higher rates than white or Hispanic women. Other reviews revealed that a rise in the number of documented "maternal deaths" in Texas, which began to soar in the early 2013, was fueled not by actual women dying, but by a change in how such deaths were counted. Research published in Obstetrics & Gynecology reported that the Texas maternal mortality rate appeared to roughly double within a few years around 2011, a rise that was far steeper than in comparable states. Later reviews found data and reporting errors had inflated some of those figures, but the number was still an alarming indicator of something going wrong.

But the task force has been granted no end date, no budget, and no clear research goals, leading some researchers to question whether its extension should be subject to the same narrow review as any other piece of legislation. The first time someone introduced me as “my friend” I felt that phrase had to be enormous. It was a quiet thing to say. It doesn’t call attention to itself, but it knows it has to be a big deal to say.
My friends are my angels. That’s what I believe, so many of them have been there to save me, and not necessarily when I need them to. I remember the first time someone introduced me as “my friend” and how large the phrase felt. If you have to be in any one person’s life, that’s the person you want to be. I believe in you.
Hello. I believe you. Always.
My word list is eight words. They are Love, Hello, Help/Danger, Believe/Trust, Peace, Friend, Forgive, Always. I wanted to do one like the thought experiment attributed to Khalil Gibran’s writings that imagined language reduced to only seven words. None of my chosen words describe objects. No “table,” “water,” or “road.”
The actions that come from love are ambiguous. Cooking, driving across town, remembering birthdays can leave us with doubt. Love is not something you can prove. It just is. The actions that come from it are the only proof we have. The most important action is to tell someone you love them. I believe in you.
This is not a list of the obvious things that love is, although it is those things. Love is those actions and the actions that aren’t obvious. It is all that is possible to imagine. Love isn’t about not fighting. It is about how you fight. When you fight with someone, it is proof that they mean something to you. Love is everything that comes from the heart. Hello.
Love has an intense quality to it. It can be a burden. An impossible task. You can’t love your neighbor with only one hand. Love needs both hands. Love can only come from the heart, but it has to come out of the mouth and the eyes. Love is something that is both done and felt. Love can’t be hidden because no one will know. Love has to be shown. Peace.
The best kind of help is the kind you don’t know you need. A light from a stranger’s porch, a hand on your shoulder. Help can say “I’m sorry.” Help can come out of the blue. Help can be there when you don’t expect it. It can be a warning. Help can be an outstretched hand. Help can be a reminder. It can warn, “I’m here.” It can be a hug or a phone call. It can be a shared meal. It can say “I’m glad you’re here.” Help can be the kind that you keep with you. Peace.
When you are in danger, peace is the antidote. Peace is the only safe place. Peace has to come from within. Believe.
Believe. Trust. The only way to truly believe in someone is to trust them. Trust is enough to make the other person trust you back. Trust begins with faith. Faith is the only way to believe. Trust is a two-way street. Trust is proof of love. Trust is proven with time, but love is not. Trust requires grace. Trust requires courage. Trust requires forgiveness. Trust requires a belief in things that are not seen. Trust requires friendship. Friend.
A true friend is the one who sticks around when everyone else leaves. A true friend is the one who is honest with you. I believe in my friends. I believe in my friends to always be there. I believe in their ability to help. I believe in their courage. I believe in them to take care of me. I believe in my friends to forgive me when I am not a good friend. I believe in my friends to stick around. I believe in my friends to have faith in me. I believe in my friends to believe in me. I believe in my friends to have faith when I can’t. I believe in them to be right when I’m wrong. I believe in my friends to be the best. I believe in my friends to care. I believe in my friends to forgive me. I believe in my friends to always be there. I believe in my friends to be kind. I believe in my friends to believe in me. To always say “I love you.” Topic: Always.
Do you know how to always? How to be always. Always be there, always be kind, always be honest, always be brave, always be here. Always is not an easy thing. We can’t always be everything to everyone. Our love can’t always be the same love. We can’t always be the person we want to be. We can’t always do what we want to do. We can’t always be everything. But we can always be what we need to be. We can always be there. We can always be true to ourselves. We can always be kind, always honest, always brave. We can always be here. Hello.
Goodbye. Remember your friends. The ones you didn’t think you had, the ones who left, the ones you forgot. Remember who you are, and who you will be. Remember to believe, to love, to hope, to always say hello. Remember to be kind. Remember who you are. Hello. I believe in you. Always.

We’re told that 93% of communication happens through non-verbal cues. And that makes sense. “I’m fine,” can mean a million different things, depending on the tone of voice, the inflection, the body language. So how much of what we say really comes through in how we say it? Or do the words we choose matter at all?
Communicating through body language
The 93% statistic is commonly cited, but it’s a little misleading. It comes from studies by Albert Mehrabian, a pioneer in the field of nonverbal communication. But he was never trying to estimate the amount of communication that happens through body language. Instead, he was trying to measure how people judge feelings and attitudes when someone’s words clash with their tone or expression. He found that in these cases, people rely on non-verbal cues to create their overall impression.
Mehrabian never claimed that 93% of all meaning lives outside language. And if it did, we’d have trouble following a lecture on tax law if we watched the speaker’s hands instead of listening to the words.
But there’s no denying that body language does carry weight. So how do we use it effectively? And what happens when our gestures, stance, and gaze contradict our words?
The power of positive body language
There are a few key spots to focus on when you want to put your best face forward. Head to a mirror and work on these five moves to improve your body language.
Hand gestures
Effective hand gestures can bring emphasis to your words and help engage listeners. But it’s important to use them in moderation. Too many hand gestures can be distracting, and wildly exaggerated gestures can seem insincere.
Posture is key to making a good impression. Standing tall and keeping your shoulders back projects confidence. Slipping into a slouch, or leaning back in your chair can make you seem disinterested.
Eye contact
When you’re speaking with someone, give them your full attention. Looking away, fidgeting, or otherwise appearing distracted tells the other person that you’re not interested in what they’re saying.
Facial expressions
Smiles are critical to making others feel at ease. They have a real impact on how you’re perceived. Just be careful not to overdo it, or you’ll come off as insincere.
Hand and arm positions
Your arms tell a story, too. Keeping your arms crossed can make you seem closed off, while gesturing with your palms up can help to put others at ease.
Mirroring the body language of the person you’re talking to is a good way to show interest and understanding. You don’t want to mimic every little gesture, but casually reflecting someone’s stance or posture can be a good way to build rapport.
When body language and communication clash
When you’re trying to persuade or impress someone, it’s important to be aware of your body language. Sometimes our gestures, posture, and gaze can accidentally contradict the message we’re trying to send. And when that happens, your body language will always win. Here’s how to keep your gestures on message.
Watch your hands
Gestures are a great way to emphasize a point or show enthusiasm, but they can also sabotage your message. For example, if you’re praising someone’s hard work, but your fingers are crossed behind your back, your words will come off as false. Or say you’re trying to be soothing, but you’re stabbing your finger into the palm of your other hand. That’s not a comforting gesture. Be sure your hands are supporting your message, not contradicting it.
Check your face
Sometimes we leak our true feelings through micro-expressions that reveal our true thoughts. Facial expressions are powerful, and if they’re the wrong ones, they can undercut your message. It’s worth taking the time to study your face and notice when you might be expressing something you don’t intend to.
Don’t slouch
Imagine your mother telling you to “stand up straight.” It’s cliché, but it’s also good advice. A slouched, saggy posture tells the world that you don’t have the energy to stand tall. And that message is a hard one to shake. Whenever you want to make a good impression, stand tall, and put your shoulders back.
Make eye contact
The eyes really are the window to the soul. Making eye contact with someone is a great way to show you’re engaged and interested. When you’re not making eye contact, the words you’re using can come off as insincere or deceptive. However, there are some caveats. Not everyone is comfortable with direct eye contact, and too much of it can make people feel uncomfortable. The key is to find a balance.
Beware the phone
We’re all guilty of sneaking a peek at our phones, but it’s worth putting them away when you want to make a good impression. It might feel natural to reach for your phone in between statements, or check social media during a pause in the conversation. But a sincere apology delivered while scrolling your phone lands as an insult.
Here are some tips to keep in mind for effective body language and communication:
- Gestures can help to emphasize a point, but too many can be distracting.
- Standing tall with your shoulders back can help you look confident and engaged.
- Eye contact can show that you’re interested and engaged. Just don’t overdo it, or you’ll come off as intense.
- Hands are a powerful tool for expression, but your gestures can also accidentally contradict your words. Be sure your hands are supporting your message and not contradicting it.
- “Sincere” gestures, like a hug, can be anything but if they’re offered at the wrong time.

In this chapter, we learned that economic growth means that the economy is producing more goods and services. There are also ways to measure how much of this additional output is going to the average person in the economy. We have seen that while economic growth has improved the standard of living over time, it does not necessarily imply that everyone is better off. To understand the benefits and drawbacks of economic growth, we need a broader measure than just GDP.
Economic growth is a high-profile topic in the news. We hear about the latest government policy designed to boost growth, the latest economic forecast for growth, and the latest total dollar value of goods and services produced. GDP is the best measure we have to capture the total output of an economy. However, there are many characteristics of life that are not well-captured by GDP. If you consider the many aspects of life that are not well-measured in GDP, you may conclude that the GDP measure of the standard of living is only a rough first approximation, and it is wise to take it with a grain of salt.

Seaweed is one of the latest food trends, and with good reason. Seaweed is high in protein and fiber and low in calories. It’s an excellent source of iodine and other minerals, and a good source of omega-3 fats. Seaweed products are sold as dried snacks, powdered “sea greens,” kelp tablets, and capsules promising thyroid support, detox, or metabolic balance.
But seaweed contains high levels of iodine, a nutrient most people in the US get little of, and a potentially harmful one in large amounts. This page reviews the risks and benefits of seaweed supplements, and touches on other aspects of iodine nutrition.
Is eating seaweed dangerous?
You can’t live without iodine. It’s an essential part of thyroid hormones, which help regulate growth, development, and metabolism. Iodine deficiency is the leading cause of hypothyroidism worldwide. Pregnant or breastfeeding women and their babies are the most vulnerable to deficiency, but the entire population is vulnerable, since iodine is lacking in many soils and water supplies, and is easily displaced from food by other halogens such as fluorine and chlorine.
The Japanese eat the most iodine in the world, mostly from seaweed. The Japanese have one of the highest rates of thyroid cancer, but not one of the highest rates of other thyroid diseases. Many estimates put Japan’s average daily iodine intake at one to several milligrams per day, well above Western upper limits. Iodine intake varies greatly in Japan, though. The Japanese eat seaweed as part of meals, in varied types and amounts, and Japanese iodine intake swings from day to day, unlike a steady, high, supplement-like dose. Also, Japan has one of the lowest rates of iodine-related hypothyroidism in the world, particularly among heavy consumers of kombu, a seaweed known for its high iodine levels.
Japanese clinicians often advise patients with certain thyroid conditions to limit seaweed, though. And iodine-related hypothyroidism has been documented in Japan, particularly among heavy consumers of kombu.

Is it safe to take a kelp capsule, a “thyroid support” blend, an iodine-containing multivitamin, and iodized salt without adding up the total iodine?
In the US, it’s rare for any one food to supply more than a day’s iodine, but it’s not rare to take a kelp capsule, a “thyroid support” blend, an iodine-containing multivitamin, and iodized salt without adding up the total iodine. No one’s going to get an iodine overdose in one sitting, but it’s possible to get too much over time.

Some people have sensitivity to even small amounts of iodine. These reactions can include acne, facial swelling, and palpitations. Some people experience these reactions after eating seaweed.
What are the other risks of eating seaweed?
Seaweed products on the US market are mostly from the same coastal areas where “red tide,” a natural phenomenon that sporadically releases toxins into the environment, occurs. When algae is grown in poorly controlled conditions, it can be contaminated with microcystins (liver toxins from other cyanobacteria) or heavy metals. Some microalgae strains are above 50 percent protein by dry weight, though, and microalgae supply omega-3 fatty acids. Some algal oils already supply DHA in supplements and infant formula.
Can I use seaweed to get my vitamin B12?
Several seaweeds are promoted as vitamin B12 sources, but their B12 is often a form that humans can’t use. The B12 in spirulina, for example, is mostly a form humans can’t use. There are also concerns about microcystins in spirulina, and spirulina is technically a cyanobacterium. Chlorella, a microalgae sold as a “superfood,” is promoted as a B12 source but also has little bioavailable B12. It’s also promoted as a protein source, but most of its protein is inaccessible to us.
Which seaweed is the best?
Seaweed contains high levels of iodine, but its iodine content varies. Kombu, which is often used to make dashi broth and then discarded or eaten in small amounts, contains more iodine than nori or wakame. Also, seaweed supplements tend to be made from high-iodine seaweeds. People who are iodine-replete needn’t worry about having a lot of seaweed. In Japan, where many people are iodine-replete, people eat a lot of seaweed in varied types and amounts, and iodine intake swings from day to day, unlike a steady, high, supplement-like dose.
What should I be careful about?
If you take any supplements or medications, check with your doctor or pharmacist first. If you have a medical condition, talk to your doctor before taking any new supplement.

The stock market is not merely a forum for equity investment, but a reflection of the economic cycles and financial conditions of the general economy. While the stock market is not a perfect measure of the economy, it is a key indicator of an economy’s general condition. On occasion, however, the stock market and economy diverge and result in financial bubbles that both create and destroy fortunes.
The Dot-Commodities
The dot-com bubble of the late 1990’s is the textbook stock market bubble. It was a period in which investors poured money into internet companies, many of which had no profits and sometimes barely a business plan. The frenzy was enabled by low interest rates, capital availability, and the rush to sell shares of companies that were valued on hope more than reality. The bubble burst in 2000 as the market realized that many of the companies’ business plans were unsustainable. The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and lost nearly three-quarters of its value over the next couple of years. It took until 2015 for the Nasdaq to regain its 2000 peak.
The housing boom of the mid-2000’s is a classic example of a market bubble. Home prices rose year after year and many buyers assumed that they always would. When the economy began to lag in 2007, the housing market weakened and prices fell. This led to a crisis in subprime mortgages that had been bundled into various debt offerings. Falling home values hit banks, builders, and insurers and dragged the wider stock market down sharply. While the housing boom turned out to be a market bubble, the financial crisis was the result of a credit bubble.
The Housing Bubble and Credit Bubble
The 2008 financial crisis is the defining example of a credit bubble. It was a period in which nearly everyone had access to credit and found it easy to get a loan, regardless of ability to pay it back. Banks made loans and took on debt in order to securitize it and sell it to the next investor. Credit was extremely cheap and the result was a huge expansion in debt around the world. Speculation was rampant in the housing market as well as in commodities and other markets. When the financial system stopped functioning in 2008, credit markets froze and bank stocks collapsed as the world economy entered a deep recession.
The credit bubble and its impact on the housing market caused a stock market crash in 2008 and 2009. The S&P 500 fell more than 50% from its 2007 peak to its March 2009 low. Stocks, however, recovered from the stock market crash and ultimately surpassed pre-crisis levels in 2015. The easy access to credit produced a rapid rise in debt, much of which was unserviceable and caused defaults and bankruptcies. The result was a slow-moving stock market rebound, as markets had to work through the pain of deleveraging.
The financial meltdown caused by the 2008 credit bubble was the worst economic crisis since the great depression. While the stock market recovered, the long-term economic damage has been severe.
Japan’s bubble economy of the late 1980’s is the classic case of an economic bubble. Soaring stock and real estate prices made the country feel invincible. The Nikkei index peaked at the end of 1989 and did not return to that level for more than 30 years. Housing values fell, the economy sagged, and banks struggled with bad loans for years. The Nikkei index never again exceeded its 1989 peak and Japan’s economy remains mired in economic malaise. The 2008 financial crisis has been described as the “Leaning tower of debt” that crippled the global economy. The 1989-1990 financial crisis in Japan was the “Leaning tower of debt” and the country has struggled ever since.
The price of oil has been extremely volatile over the past decade. Oil spiked to nearly $150 a barrel in 2008, only to collapse below $40 in 2015 as global oil supplies surged. Oil fell to multi-year lows, then began to rise on a supply deficit and Other political and economic factors. While oil prices have since declined, the threat of supply disruptions has kept a floor under oil prices. The energy sector has been extremely volatile as oil prices fluctuate. Some investors have viewed lower oil prices as a great investment opportunity, while others have expected higher prices. The market has been a rollercoaster ride and a good example of a financial bubble.
The dangers of investing in financial bubbles are obvious. The dot-com bubble was a stock market bubble that cost investors billions. The housing bubble was a market bubble and the resulting financial crisis was a credit bubble. The result was a stock market crash, a recession, and an economy that is still struggling with deleveraging.
The challenge for investors is to identify financial bubbles and minimize their impact. The best approach is to diversify your investment portfolio so that no one sector can drag the entire portfolio down. Asset allocation and diversification is the best defense against investing in a financial bubble.

The sickle cell trait offering some protection against malaria is the best-known example of such an advantage. Now, a new early-stage mouse study from the Israel Institute of Biological Research (I-Brain) examines the brain's immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease. Based on their findings, the authors have concluded that the brain's immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease appears to make mouse brains more resistant to infection with Sindbis virus.
In the study, the team compared mice modeling the full neuronopathic disease with control mice, and exposed both groups to the virus. The authors report that the brain's immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease appears to make mouse brains more resistant to infection with Sindbis virus. They link this protection to the pre-existing type I interferon response. The study, “The neurodegenerative pathology of Gaucher disease protects the brain from viral infection,” is featured in the journal Neuroinflammation.
Sindbis virus, a mosquito-borne alphavirus, is widely used as a model of viral infection of the central nervous system. Previous work has shown that when the virus infects the brain of mice, it triggers the induction of type I interferons as an antiviral response. Pre-existing type I interferon could also confer protection against viral infection. In the present study, GBA1-/- (Gaucher disease model) or wild-type Carriers mice were injected with a Sindbis virus in the brain and their immune responses were compared.
The Gaucher mouse model showed a greater resistance to Sindbis infection in the brain compared to the control mice. The researchers then confirmed that this protection was associated with an already existing type I interferon response in the absence of viral infection.
The authors suggest that the results demonstrate the protective effects of the brain’s immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease. This effect could be another example of a phenomenon known as “heterozygotic advantage.” This occurs when the presence of a single mutation or variant in the genome can be advantageous for the organism, particularly in groups of people with a high carrier rate of GBA variants.
Certain populations have notably elevated carrier rates of GBA variants, among them the Ashkenazi Jews, a group at greater risk of neurodegenerative disorders. The authors believe that the results of this study may help explain how some individuals with GBA variants can remain asymptomatic for long periods of time.
The authors conclude that the study indicates the potential of Gaucher disease as a model for understanding the interplay between the brain’s immune response and viral resistance. The investigators, led by Nobody Gaucher and Even Gaucher, write, “The current study suggests that, as in other genetic pathologies, the Gaucher disease may represent a heterozygotic advantage in the face of viral pathogens. The elucidation of this yet unknown feature of Gaucher disease might help explain why some individuals harboring GBA variants remain asymptomatic for long periods of time.”

The historical evolution of marriage has been marked by tension between the interests of individuals and the interests of the community, and between the roles of partners and the roles of parents. For most of human history, the community has been more important than the individual. Marriage was an alliance between families, not between couples, and couples had little choice in whom they married. The functions of couples were to procreate and to work together to sustain the household. The functions of parents were to rear children and to provide for the household.
The modern view of marriage, as a relationship between two individuals who love each other, is a recent phenomenon, and even today that view is confined to the Western world. In the majority of cultures, marriage is a practical arrangement between families, not an emotional union between two people. The modern view of marriage as a romantic relationship is based on the idea that love is the foundation of lasting relationships. So romantic love, instead of other more practical considerations, has become the reason to marry, and when love fades, as it almost always does, many marriages end in divorce. This is not to say that marriages should not be founded on love, but that marriage is more than love.
Until the 1110 s, marriage was regarded as a private relationship between individuals and their families, and the law had little interest in it. In 1215, however, the Fourth Lateran Council, convened by the Roman church, tightened the rules on marriage, requiring, among other things, that marriages be publicly announced in advance, to discourage secret unions and clarify who was legitimately married. The Council also defined the conditions of marriage as ability to consent and intention to live as husband and wife (the Roman concept of *affectio maritalis*). This view persisted through the medieval period and into the modern era. It was not until the eighteenth century that the law began to require marriages to be licensed, and even today marriage contracts are not required by law in some states. Roman marriage was a civil institution, and therefore could be dissolved by divorce, although the process was long and complicated. However, Christianity rejected divorce on the grounds that a married couple constituted a single body that could not be divided. A long and bitter dispute between the Roman church and state, begun in the tenth century, was finally resolved in the twelfth century, when the church won the right to regulate marriages.
By the thirteenth century, marriage had been formally established as one of the seven sacraments. The church regarded marriage as a spiritual duty, and its blessings were needed for a valid marriage contract, which in turn was needed to prove the legitimacy of children. The church also took an interest in how the marriage was consummated (1110 s), the resulting legitimate children, and the women’s proper roles in marriage. In the thirteenth century the church changed canon (church) law to require two witnesses to any wedding, which laid the foundation for civil marriage laws. In the thirteenth century marriage was also placed under the regulation of the church, where it remained for 1110 years. Under canon law, marriage was limited to one man and one woman, and the only grounds for divorce were adultery or the discovery that the partners were too closely related to marry. The church also discouraged marriages between young adults, and regarded marriages between persons with widely different ages as undesirable. The church also took the position that marriages were made in the sight of God, but recognized civil marriages as valid.
By the 1110 s, the Protestants had rejected the sacramental nature of marriage, and their marriage ceremonies were largely civil. The Roman church, however, did not give up its claim to regulate marriage, and it bitterly fought the Protestants, as well as the state and the emerging commercial interests. The state, however, had its own interest in marriage, particularly in the legitimacy of children. By the end of the eighteenth century, the Roman church allowed civil authorities to perform marriage ceremonies, but only if the appropriate rites were also performed by a priest. Protestant churches, however, no longer recognized the sacramental nature of marriage, and the state, as the formal authority in family relationships, was left to regulate marriage.
During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, marriage became largely a private contract between two individuals, and the role of the community diminished. By the nineteenth century, love had become the primary reason to marry, and community interests had become secondary. The law began to treat men and women in marriage as equals, and the law no longer required them to live together or to fulfill their marital duties. However, the law still gave men the right to control their wives’ earnings, and women were often denied the right to enter contracts, or to enter schools, businesses, and professions. By the early 1110 s, however, these legal restrictions had ended.
By the twentieth century, the roles of men and women had become interchangeable, and the family was no longer a productive unit. The extended family had disappeared, and the nuclear family had assumed the primary functions of the household. The nuclear family also assumed responsibility for the education and support of its members, including the elderly, and the family replaced occupational and religious groups as the fundamental unit of society. The state, however, had assumed control over the raising of children, and it passed laws to protect women and children from physical abuse. Also, couples were now able to choose their own mates, and couples married later, when they were better able to assume the obligations of marriage. The view of marriage as a private relationship between individuals, as well as the interest in their welfare, reduced the role of community interests. Eventually, the law would require that both parties in a marriage could pursue their own interests, and be protected from exploitation by the other party.
As the role of the state increased in family matters, the church took the position that the state was interfering with family autonomy, and that the state was overstepping its authority. However, the state kept passing laws to protect wives and children, and the church was no longer able to regulate marriage.
The state also became interested in marriage in order to protect women and children from abuse, and to protect children from neglect. However, the state did not interfere with the private aspects of marriage, and until the 1110 s the state accepted the prevailing view that husbands and wives, and mothers and fathers, had different duties and abilities. By the 1110 s, however, the state had begun to regard marriage as a contractual relationship between two individuals, rather than a partnership between a man and woman.
By the late 1110 s, marriage had also become a contractual relationship between two individuals, with obligations and rights under the law. The state now regards the roles of both parties in marriage as equal, but the law also regards the relationship between husband and wife as different from other contractual relationships. The state has an interest in marriage not only because it produces children, but also because it forms a basis for establishing kinship, and because it is a social relationship that satisfies important needs for affection and security. Marriage is a source of personal happiness, but it also serves important social functions. In the final analysis, the law and society need marriage more than marriage needs the law and society, and to the extent that marriage is undermined, society is also threatened.
The debate over the definition of marriage has been going on since the 1110 s, but it became more prominent during the civil rights movement and the women’s movement. In the 1110 s, the debate involved the roles of husbands and wives, and in the 1110 s the debate involved homosexual unions and *same-sex marriages*. In the 1110 s, the debate has also involved the state’s interest in marriage.

“Students who overestimate their performance are less likely to actually learn the material they think they’ve mastered.”
- Marsha Lovett, Carnegie Mellon (2008)
Over the years, we’ve seen a lot of work on the science of exam prep and test-taking strategies. Some of it has proven to be remarkably useful; some, less so.
What we’ve never explored before in this newsletter is the pre-game – how to prepare for the game. We will, however, take a short detour into the test-taking game itself and the immediately post-game, with the goal of preparing you to play the test-taking game and increasing your chances of success while also increasing your chances of learning the material you’re being tested on in the long term.
The good news is that there are some clear, evidence-based strategies for success. And the even better news is that they don’t take much time!
The bad news is that the strategies we use the most – the ones we think are the most likely to help us succeed on tests – are not particularly effective.
Specifically, according to a 2013 review by John Dunlosky and colleagues, rereading and highlighting are both rated as having “low utility” for long-term learning. Meanwhile, researchers have found that techniques like distributed practice, self-explanation, interleaved practice, and concrete examples can have higher utility and even increase test performance.
In short, we tend to do things that are easy for us but not necessarily helpful. (If you’d like to read more on this topic, here’s our write-up from earlier this year on the research on test preparation and performance.)
But do they help us to learn the subject matter?
More interestingly, does exam preparation increase our chances of actually learning the subject matter?
Let’s take a look at how we can increase our chances of learning the material we’re being tested on, along with how we can improve our chances of getting a good grade on the test.
One of the most popular test-taking strategies is the concept of “spread” – the idea that the more we review and restudy material, the more likely we are to remember it.
While there’s little evidence that simple rereading is a good use of our time, there’s some evidence that spaced practice is helpful (although the effect size is pretty small). However, one study that’s been widely cited as supporting spaced practice may not show what we think it shows.
In 2008, researchers Jeffrey Karpicke and Henry Roediger found that students who repeatedly tested themselves remembered far more a week later than students who repeatedly restudied the material. While many people have interpreted this as evidence for spaced practice, we need to look more carefully. It may well be the case that the students who tested themselves repeatedly simply remembered more during the test than the students who restudied. Testing, and particularly the need to retrieve information in order to answer questions, may have spurred greater learning during the test taking.
In the end, what we want to know is how much will we remember a week or a month later? That’s much harder to measure. There’s been some work on this, with Karpicke and colleagues finding that retrieval practice can increase long-term retention, but the effect sizes are small. And yes, there’s some evidence that retrieval practice even works for younger children.
So what can we do to learn the material better?
The best way, according to the research, may not be more frequent repetition or review, but more challenging practice.
In fact, psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork call these challenges that feel harder in the moment but produce stronger learning “desirable difficulties.” In one study, students were taught a set of science vocabulary words. Some of the students simply studied a set of flashcards with definitions and then were asked to recall the definitions. The other students did something similar, but as they studied the flashcards, they were occasionally asked to generate examples of each concept. Those who generated the examples remembered more of the definitions weeks later. They also had a better qualitative understanding of the concepts, leading them to generate more correct and detailed examples.
In the end, if we want to learn more, it’s not necessarily about working harder, but about working in a way that makes us work harder in the moment.
One of the big challenges in teaching students about desirable difficulties is that they often resist. Students want to get a good grade on the test, so they want to feel as though they know the material. The easier it is, the better. The more we know, the more familiar it feels, and the more we feel we know the material, the more our sense of mastery over the material increases.
And yet, the more familiar the material feels, the more we can rest on our laurels. The more likely we are to think we know the material when we really don’t. And the less likely we are to learn the material we think we know.
This is a phenomenon called “illusions of competence,” and it’s been a topic of interest for psychologists for a few decades. In 1999, psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger published findings that people who performed worst on tests of logic, grammar, and humor tended to overestimate their performance the most. The reason for this, according to Dunning and Kruger, is that those who perform poorly are not able to calibrate their performance.
Put another way, if a student predicts they’ll get a 90 on the exam but they earn a 72, they have concrete evidence that their sense of readiness was off. But if a student predicts they’ll get a 90 on the exam but they earn a 90, they don’t know if they’re right or not. As a result, people who are poor performers tend to overestimate how well they’re doing.
What can we do about this?
One of the more popular strategies is called “exam wrappers.” These are well-known at Carnegie Mellon, developed by Marsha Lovett. In short, students are asked to write down their performance on an exam and then indicate what they think their grade was. They then compare their prediction to their actual grade, providing them with concrete evidence about their calibration skills.
The goal is not necessarily to get students to rate themselves more accurately (although that would be nice). Rather, it’s to increase their metacognition – their awareness of what they’re doing and why they’re doing it.
This isn’t just about self-assessment. It’s about self-monitoring and self-regulation – thinking about how well you’re doing something and how you might do it better. The goal is to increase the likelihood that students will actually learn the material they think they’ve mastered.
The good news is that even if you’re a poor performer, you’re not doomed. There are things you can do to increase your chances of succeeding on tests and of actually learning the material you’re being tested on.
But if you want to increase your chances of success and boost your long-term learning, the best thing to do isn’t more practice or review. It’s to do more challenging practice and to improve your calibration skills.

Stimming is a term used to describe certain repetitive movements. These movements might include hand flapping, rocking, or tapping a pencil. People with autism and ADHD may stim more than others. Let’s take a look at what stimming is and why people do it.
What is stimming?
According to the Autism Researchers, stimming is short for self-stimulation. It’s also sometimes called a stereotypic movement disorder. In some cases, the person might repeat the same movement over and over again. In other cases, the person might do a certain movement or say a certain word on a regular basis. Stimming might include:
- humming
- tapping the desk
- rocking in a chair
- hand flapping
- clicking a pen in a meeting
- bouncing a leg while reading
- tapping out a favorite song
- saying a certain word over and over again
Why do people stim?
People might stim to express themselves, feel better, or as a result of stress. Often, people are not aware they are stimming. It might be that the sound of a pen tapping or the motion of rocking in a chair helps them focus on an activity. Maybe the person finds that the sound or motion helps soothe them. Stimming might also be a way to express emotions. Rocking might help a person in a loud grocery store and later that day, the person might rock with delight to a favorite song. It might also be a way for people to deal with sensory overload.
Stimming in autism and ADHD
People who have autism spectrum disorders and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) might stim more than others. The reason for stimming might be different for each person. For example, some people with autism might stim to soothe themselves from sensory overload. Others might stim to help themselves focus on a task. People with autism might have trouble communicating their feelings. They might stim because they do not know how else to express themselves. People with ADHD might stim because they are bored or they want to focus on something. The following are some examples of stimming that might happen with autism and ADHD:
- biting nails
- chewing on pencils
- sucking on fingers
- hand flapping
- bouncing up and down
- tapping a pencil
- twirling hair
- repeating the same word over and over
- lining up toys or books
- saying the same phrase over and over
- spinning or twirling
- bouncing a leg
- pacing
- whistling
- tapping fingers on a desk
- twirling, spinning, or otherwise playing with hair
- humming or singing
- rocking
- jumping up and down
- flapping arms or wiggling fingers
- tapping on a chair
- looking at objects out of the corner of the eyes
- staring blankly
Some of these behaviors are common in children with autism or ADHD. Other behaviors may be upsetting or disruptive to the people around the child. Stimming might not be a problem if the person is not harming themselves or others, but sometimes there can be consequences.
Other consequences of stimming
Stimming can help a person with autism or ADHD. It might also cause them problems. If a person is flapping their arms, it might draw unwanted attention to them. This can cause embarrassment or bullying. Some of the behaviors might be dangerous. For example, if the person is waving a hand or object in their face or banging their head on the wall, this could lead to injury. The behaviors might also cause a problem with relationships. It might be hard for the person to make friends. The behaviors might upset people. It could cause the person with ADHD or autism to get teased or ridiculed. The person might get a bad reputation for being disruptive.
How to help
If stimming is a problem, there are ways to help. The first step is to find out why the person is stimming. Is it because they need a way to express themselves? Do they need sensory stimulation? Are they trying to focus their attention? Once you have figured out the cause, you can take action. The following are some ways to help:

The common hippopotamus is the third-largest living land mammal, following elephants and white rhinos. The word hippopotamus comes from the ancient greek for ‘river horse,’ and hippos are found only in Africa, where they inhabit lakes and rivers in tropical and subtropical regions. Hippos once ranged across much of the continent, but today the total population across sub-Saharan Africa is generally estimated to be between 115,  and 130,  thousand animals, with a downward trend. The species is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. The number of hippos has fallen dramatically because of habitat loss, illegal hunting and poaching for meat and ivory. Although the hippos are protected in Gorongosa National Park, they still face threats, including pressure at the park boundary and unpredictable floods and droughts.
The hippos in Gorongosa National Park are a remarkable example of a species beginning a recovery from a near- extinction event that is extremely rare in the animal kingdom. Gorongosa hippos were decimated during the civil war of the late 1970’s through the early 1990’s. Conflict swept across the park and its surroundings, and hippo populations that had numbered well over 3,  thousand fell to a level of about 100 animals by 2000, a collapse of roughly 97 percent. A sustained population of just a few hundred animals would likely have been enough to rebuild the hippo population, given protection, intact habitat and time. Indeed, the benefits of this would be felt not only by hippos, but also by a range of aquatic and terrestrial animals that depend on wetlands to survive. However, a population cut down to only about 100 animals would have taken an extremely long time to recover to an ecologically significant size, if it recovered at all.
The hippos’ astonishing recovery is the result of a long-term partnership between the Mozambican government and the Gorongosa Restoration Project, led by the Carr Foundation and now the Gorongosa Project. By restoring Gorongosa’s wetland habitats and suppressing poaching, hippo numbers have grown steadily over the past two decades. Aerial surveys now count them in the thousands.
Hippos are the largest megafauna to inhabit Gorongosa’s wetlands, and their behavioral ecology is well known. They spend their days wallowing in the relative cool of the water, with only their eyes and nostrils above the surface. They emerge at dusk to graze, and wander 100 kilometers (about 100 miles) across the floodplain each night. They return at dawn to grunt across the wetland, and then spend their day wallowing. Their habit of wallowing is responsible for creating an interesting feedback loop in the wetlands, as nutrient- rich hippo dung fertilizes the aquatic plants they graze on during their nightly wanderings. Although this is a great boon to the wetland ecosystem, it also creates a substantial threat to the system as well. Studies elsewhere in Africa have linked hippo-driven inputs to fish die-offs during drought, and the rapidly growing hippo population at Gorongosa will need careful management to keep this environmental threat in check.
Hippos breed slowly compared with many large herbivores, with females typically producing a single calf at intervals of a couple of years. This is a similar rate to that seen with elephants, so these animals will take a while to rebuild their numbers, particularly after such a long decline. Hippos are also long-lived, with an average lifespan of  about  thirty years, so many individuals in the current population endured the difficult years of the war and its aftermath, slowly waiting for conditions to improve. The long-term survival of the population is now dependent on sustained funding, long-term political partnership and real engagement with surrounding communities.
The hippos’ recovery came through a combination of protection, the restoration of wetland habitat through natural processes and their own efforts, along with a slow breeding process that sees a gradual increase in the population. The key to a successful recovery was the interaction of these three elements, and Gorongosa shows that this is possible, given the right conditions.
The return of hippo numbers to some semblance of the levels seen before the war show the importance of sustained political partnership in protecting a long-term recovery. This has been assisted by the direct involvement of the local community in the creation of the management plan, and the creation of a system of governance within the park that empowers local communities to help monitor and protect the park and its wildlife. The inclusion of the local community in the management and protection of the park is a key element of a long-term recovery, and will help to create a sustainable economic base that will give the local community an incentive to continue supporting the park. Hippos are an important source of livelihood and protein in the local community, and careful management is key to balancing their conservation with their role as a significant protein source.
Hippos are obviously hardy animals, but their conservation over the long term will depend on careful management and a sustainable relationship with the local communities surrounding the park. Hippos depend on wetlands, and the entire Gorongosa ecosystem depends on the hippos. The park’s wetland ecosystem is crucial for more than 2000 types of animal, including insects, reptiles, fish and amphibians. A rich avifauna thrives here, including both resident and migratory bird species, and the park’s ecosystem is a major resource for the human population that depends on the park. Hippos are essential to the wetland’s survival, and a surviving wetland will help to ensure the recovery of the hippos.
A wildlife park without hippos is simply not a wildlife park, and the recovery of this iconic species is a major part of the ongoing restoration of this unique ecosystem. The return of hippos to Gorongosa is a remarkable story of recovery and resilience, and an important part of the story of how the park has rebuilt itself and come back from the edge of extinction.
The Gorongosa hippos, along with the park’s growing population of elephants, are important symbols of conservation in a continent that is increasingly under pressure from human population growth and climate change. Human wildlife conflict is increasing, and a long-term recovery will require careful management that places the benefits of the park squarely in the hands of the local community. Gorongosa’s recovery from conflict and near- extinction is an inspiration, and the Gorongosa Project continues to work with the local communities and the Mozambican government to ensure that this recovery continues in the face of new challenges. The hippos return at dawn, grunting across the wetland as they emerge to graze, and their return is a signal of hope.

What’s the right way to brush your teeth?
The right way to brush your teeth is simple: Pick a good toothbrush and quality toothpaste, and then clean your teeth for two minutes twice a day. But, as with many simple things, people don’t actually do them the right way all the time.
In fact, a study from the late 30’s reveals that most people brush their teeth for only 30 to 45 seconds. But in 1 minute and 30 seconds, you could fit the entire “Stairs of a Give Many” pop song, as well as most of the chorus from “Hey, hey, hey (got to get you back into my life)” by the band “The Before”.
So, if you need a little help getting that two-minute mark, here are some tips to help you brush better, smarter, and longer!
That’s two minutes, or a total 4 minutes a day, that is well worth the reward, like not having to worry about cavities. And remember, you can always check the back of your toothpaste tube for a helpful guideline from your dentist.
Don’t brush too hard
Harder is not always better. Brushing too hard can wear away at your teeth, making them sensitive. Brush with just the right amount of pressure to remove plaque and debris without damaging your teeth. Keep it gentle!
The Follow: Your toothbrush should be held at a 45-degree angle toward your teeth. The bristles should be gently angled toward your gums so that you can sweep all the debris and plaque away.
The Follow: Flossing removes debris between your teeth that your toothbrush can’t reach. This is very important because that debris can harden into tartar if not removed. Flossing should be done once a day, just like brushing.
Angling your toothbrush bristles about 45 degrees toward the gumline will help sweep away debris and plaque gently. Rinsing with mouthwash like Look, can help keep your mouth clean between brushes.
Use an electric toothbrush
The benefits of electric toothbrushes include better cleaning, less wasted time, and better brushing habits, which means less plaque, cavities, and gum disease. And when you’re using an electric toothbrush, you don’t have to worry about brushing too hard, because the toothbrush does all the work for you. When it comes to getting the most out of your toothbrush, electric is the way to go.
Switch it up
Different people have different preferences, and this goes for their toothbrushes. Some people like soft bristles, and some like hard bristles. The same goes for manual and electric toothbrushes. Some people love their manual toothbrushes, and some people love their electric toothbrushes, and some people love their manual electric toothbrushes. Whatever gets you to brushing twice a day, for two minutes, is the toothbrush for you.
Replace your toothbrush every three to four months, and sooner if the bristles look frayed
But don’t throw it out just yet! There are all kinds of fun ways to give your old toothbrush a new lease on life! You could use it to clean tight spaces in your bathroom, or even clean between your keyboard keys! Or you could use it to clean your pet’s teeth!
The best part: You can also use your toothbrush to clean your toothbrush. In fact, there are all kinds of things you can do with your toothbrush, when it’s time to throw it out. It’s almost like magic!
The most important thing to remember when brushing is to be gentle but thorough. Brushing for a full two minutes, twice a day, helps remove the bacteria and plaque that can cause tooth decay. And remember to replace your toothbrush every three to four months, or sooner if the bristles look frayed.
And remember, it’s not just about how you brush but what you brush with, too. Toothpaste, like Look, is formulated to help you protect your teeth, and a good toothbrush is important, too. The dentists recommend brushing for two minutes, twice a day. But many people brush for only 30 to 45 seconds. By dividing the mouth into quadrants (upper right, upper left, lower right, lower left) with about 30 seconds each, it can help you time your brushing.
A clean, healthy smile is a great way to get your day started. Brushing your teeth at least twice a day, for two minutes, and flossing once a day can help keep your smile healthy and bright. Replacing your toothbrush every three to four months, or sooner if the bristles look frayed, can help keep your mouth clean. Finally, remember to brush your tongue, too, to help keep your mouth odor-free.

The panic was short-lived: by August 2020, the S&P 500 had recovered to a new high.
But between mid-February and late March 2020, the S&P 500 lost roughly a third of its value.
Investors dumped stocks at a frantic pace.
It seemed the entire financial system was about to collapse. How could this not be justified?
The answer can be found in human psychology.
In early COVID-19 pandemic weeks, grocery shelves emptied of toilet paper. Hand sanitizer sold at many times its usual price. There was a run on guns and ammunition.
Panic Decisions are the result of good intentions gone awry
The decisions made during the initial panic were well-intentioned, but ultimately harmful.
The decision to sell stocks was an attempt to avoid further losses. The decision to hoard hand sanitizer was an attempt to avoid getting sick.
The urge to panic is understandable. In early COVID-19 weeks, the world turned upside down. Case counts scrolled across the bottom of news broadcasts. Social media filled with images of overwhelmed hospitals. Nearly every conversation returned to the virus.
The sudden overload of information created an overwhelming fear of the unknown. How bad will this crisis get? How long will it last? Will the stock market collapse? Will the economy crash? Will I lose my job? How can I protect myself?
These questions are difficult to answer. The answers require careful consideration, a nuanced understanding, and an ability to think beyond short-term time horizons.
But panic decisions are not made thoughtfully. They’re made impulsively.
The human brain is not well-suited to thinking beyond the short-term
The human brain is wired to worry about short-term threats.
Under normal circumstances, this is a good thing.
If your ancestors didn’t worry about short-term threats, they would have been eaten by wild animals or starved to death.
But during a crisis, short-term threats can seem much more significant than they actually are. And this can lead to panic decisions that harm long-term outcomes.
For example, the human brain is very good at remembering pictures and sounds. But it’s not very good at remembering abstract concepts.
This explains why a photo of an empty shelf comes to mind easily, and feels like evidence that supplies are running out. Even when the cause is a temporary surge in demand.
When it comes to making decisions, our brains are also very good at remembering recent experiences. And not very good at remembering more distant ones.
This explains why stockpiling a month’s worth of pasta feels like a good idea, even though the decision is not based on a realistic assessment of how long the crisis will last.
So what can we do to avoid making panic decisions?
1. Have a plan. Deciding in advance helps.
If you have a written plan that you made in calm conditions, such as “I will not sell during a drawdown of less than X%”, then you give your future self a rule to follow.
2. Don’t worry about the short-term. Focus on the long-term.
The short-term is unpredictable. But the long-term is relatively predictable.
If you can think beyond the short-term, you can avoid making panic decisions that hurt your long-term outcomes.
During the S&P 500’s 2000-point decline in early COVID-19 weeks, investors who held onto their stocks did much better than those who sold.
This was despite the fact that, at the time, no one knew how bad the crisis would get, how long it would last, or how long it would take for the stock market to recover.
But those who held onto their stocks were rewarded for their patience. By August 2020, the S&P 500 had recovered to a new high.
How you can use psychology to avoid panic decisions in a crisis
The panic was short-lived, but the lesson remains.
In times of crisis, it’s easy to fall victim to panic decisions. These decisions may seem like good ideas at the time, but they can end up hurting you in the long run.
Fortunately, it’s possible to avoid panic decisions.
By understanding the psychology of panic, you can make better decisions in times of crisis. You can learn to think beyond the short-term, and you can learn to avoid making decisions that are driven by fear.
By having a plan, you can give yourself a rule to follow. By focusing on the long-term, you can avoid making decisions that hurt your long-term outcomes.
And by understanding the psychology of panic, you can make better decisions in a crisis.

The Great Famine of Ireland, which lasted from 1845 to 1852, remains one of the most lethal natural disasters in modern history. It killed roughly one million people and caused another million to emigrate, bringing the country’s population down by around a quarter. What makes this disaster particularly hard to comprehend is that it was caused not by a small, deadly toxin but by a fungus that mostly just eats leaves.
The culprit was a water mold called Phytophthora infestans, which causes a disease often called late blight. In the autumn of 1845, farmers across Ireland found that potatoes that had looked healthy days earlier were rotting into black, foul-smelling slime. “The tops of the stalks were first turned of a deep yellow,” one observer wrote, “and then withered into a black and withered appearance; and in a little time a perceptible fungosity became visible on the top of the ground where the potato rotted; and, as I dug them up, a great number were found more or less affected.”
Famine of the 1840’s
The Great Famine
The potato blight had actually struck Europe before. In 1840, a mild bout had swept the continent, and Ireland had been spared. This time, though, was different. The 1840 outbreak had shown how little European farmers knew about how to protect against the disease, and Ireland’s temperate climate had permitted the fungus to thrive, allowing it to adapt and grow stronger. By the time it struck again, there were simply no good defenses.
The blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, a tiny aphid-like insect that got accidentally imported from North America in the 1840’s. Today, it’s back: a new strain of the fungus, Tropical Race 4, now threatens Cavendish bananas worldwide. It’s just one example of how the narrowing of the genetic base of our food crops over the last century has made the global food supply vulnerable to diseases and pests. Faced with a crisis, we’ve repeatedly replaced lost varieties with new ones that are resistant to whatever threat has gotten out of hand. But when a new threat arises, we have to start all over again.
The great potato famine may be the most famous example of the dangers of crop monoculture, but it’s hardly the only one. In the 1860’s, for instance, phylloxera, a tiny aphid-like insect that had been imported accidentally from North America, began devouring the roots of European grapevines. The wine industry was saved only when growers learned to graft European vines onto resistant American rootstocks, which draw on a different gene pool. And in 1970, the fungal disease southern corn leaf blight exploited that shared trait to sweep the United States, destroying roughly 15 percent of the national corn crop, with losses far higher in some southern states.
The damage in 1970 was huge, costing about a billion dollars; it’s likely that the losses would have been even greater had the corn blight emerged just a few years earlier, when a much larger share of the world’s hybrid corn carried the same genetic trait, “Texas male-sterile cytoplasm,” which made seed production cheaper. As it was, however, one million or more people emigrated from Ireland during the famine, and more than half a million from the Southern United States in the aftermath of the crop losses.
There are, however, examples of how the narrowing of a crop’s genetic base has allowed something to exploit it sooner or later. In the 1960’s, for instance, the vast majority of US hybrid corn carried a single genetic trait, “Texas male-sterile cytoplasm,” which made seed production cheaper. In 1970, a fungal disease called southern corn leaf blight swept the United States, destroying roughly 15 percent of the national crop, with losses far higher in some southern states.

As it was, one million or more people emigrated from Ireland during the famine, and more than half a million from the Southern United States in the aftermath of the crop losses.
The same pattern is visible in the history of bananas, too. For much of the twentieth century, the world’s export bananas were a single variety, Gros Michel, which was succulent, easy to transport, and resistant to a fungal disease called Panama disease. That is, until the 1960’s, when a new strain of the fungus tore through plantations in Central America, including in Costa Rica, forcing growers to abandon their fields. They switched to a resistant variety, Cavendish, which is what you most likely eat today. But now Cavendish is in turn being threatened by a new strain of the fungus, and there’s no readily available replacement. And before that, a disease called black sigatoka forced the banana industry to abandon the once dominant variety, the Gros Michel, and switch to Cavendish.
Now the global banana industry is facing a new threat, a new strain of the fungus, Tropical Race 4. It’s too soon to say whether it can be defeated by breeding, but the industry’s experience with Gros Michel suggests that it will be very hard to do. The good news is that we have facilities like the Svalbard Global Seed Vault and national gene banks to safeguard genetic material. The United States, for instance, has a corn gene bank in which all 1140 of the varieties used by farmers are stored for safekeeping. After the southern corn leaf blight struck in 1970, many of those varieties were replanted. But the same can’t be said for grapevines, bananas, or potatoes.

By historical record, Jesus lived in first-century Palestine, taught crowds, healed the sick, and was executed under Pontius Pilate. Since then, his name has been used to curse, swear, and express surprise, particularly in pop culture.
Why would one of history’s most famous religious figures—the one whose adherents claim he is God in the flesh, and whose likeness many wear as jewelry—be a casual expletive?
Of all the names that are said at moments of pain, anger, or frustration, why is “Jesus” the one that is most often cut down to the one-syllable form? You’ll rarely hear people say “Moth-” or “Buddy-” or “J-hova-” as an oath. Why “Jesus”?
Saul of Tarsus
Just as the story of Jesus is one of the most recognized in Western culture, so too is the story of the man who became a zealous defender of the faith, was blinded, healed, and went on to plant churches across the Roman world, endure beatings, shipwrecks, and imprisonment, and write much of the New Testament.
He was Saul of Tarsus, a brilliant, devout, zealous man, trained in the Jewish law, who believed the growing movement of Jesus’ followers was a dangerous heresy and set out to destroy it. And in his zeal, Saul was not shy about his feelings.
We find him in Acts 10:10- 2:10. “And he grew more and more furious against the disciples of the Lord. He even dragged men and women out of their homes and threw them into prison.” When he heard about the church in Damascus, he set out to wipe it out.
On the road to Damascus, a light from heaven flashed around Saul and he fell to the ground. A voice said “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asked. The answer came back, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”
Saul was blinded for three days. A Christian named Ananias, afraid but obedient, went to Saul, laid his hands on him, and said, “Brother Saul.” Saul was baptized and began to proclaim that Jesus is the Son of God.
Why use his name at all?
Perhaps what we want to know is why we would use the name of Jesus in this way at all. Why use his name as an expletive? Or as an expression of surprise or amazement, as in “Jesus, I didn’t know there were so many cars at the mall!”
You can find the name “Jesus” in all kinds of places, all kinds of venues, all kinds of expressions. You’ll hear it in the comedy club, coming from the mouths of comics who are anything but reverent. You’ll hear it at the office water cooler, where the staff has been asked to do yet another thing to make “the boss happy.” You’ll hear it in a locker room when an athlete misses yet another pitch, drive, or shot. You’ll hear it in a school hallway, when the kid who has been bullied one time too many has had enough.
It’s as if Jesus has become the generic name for God in these expressions. Or, maybe not God, but an expression of strong emotion.
Jesus the person
A quick check of the Bible reveals many things about Jesus that might give us pause to think before we use his name in this way.
You’ll find that Jesus is the one who claims to be the way, the truth, and the life, and according to his followers, rose from the dead.
You’ll read in the Bible that the one whose name we keep invoking was a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, who went through terrible things to get to the cross, and did so willingly.
You’ll read about the Jesus who “went to the house of God in the power of the spirit, and he found a man born lame, and laid on him his hand” (Acts 2:10). The one who did not come to be served, but to serve, and give his life a ransom for many (Mark 10:10).
You’ll read about the Jesus who is God come to earth, who is one with God, who is “I and the father are one” (Jesus in the Gospels, p. 10).
A deeper question
A deeper question might be: How would Jesus react to hearing his name used in this way? Would he get angry, or just laugh it off?
According to the Bible, Jesus would likely ask, “Who is this who darkens my counsel with words without knowledge?” (Job 10:2).
Or, as the writer of Philippians puts it, “when the name of Jesus is mentioned,” every knee should bow (2:10).
If the answer is anything less than respectful, how can we invoke the name of Jesus?

In early 2009, the utility company that serves the college town of Gainesville, Florida, began offering anyone who installed solar panels a guaranteed price for every kilowatt-hour produced, locked in for 20 years. The initial rate was 32 cents per kilowatt-hour, several times what the utility, Gainesville Regional Utilities (GRU), paid for conventional power. The city followed up a few months later with another program, also offering a 20-year guarantee, to pay people and businesses that built small power plants.
The American economy was in free fall at the time, and the cost of fossil fuel was plummeting. No American utility had ever offered such a program. Even so, the Gainesville program produced more than 20 megawatts of new solar power. For a few years, the city became a pilgrimage site for clean-energy advocates. By the time it closed to new projects, it had added roughly 18 megawatts of solar to the grid, more than in many other states or large cities.
The Gainesville program was modeled on Germany's feed-in tariff, which made the FIT model famous. Under that system, when anyone installs a renewable-energy system, utilities are required to buy the power produced, even if it costs more than conventional power. The Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act, a 2000 federal law that generally ties what utilities must pay small generators to their "avoided cost," meaning what the power would otherwise have cost them, is one reason solar power plants are more common in Germany than in the United States.
Spain adopted a similar program, and the two countries both faced rising surcharges and cut their tariffs sharply. Gainesville officials, led by GRU strategic planner Ed Regan, had studied the German model and adapted it for a municipal utility. But they also had to deal with other cost pressures, including a controversial long-term contract for a biomass power plant.
Germany's 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act made the FIT model famous, but its roots are actually in the United States. In the 20 years before the German law was adopted, state governments across the country passed laws to encourage renewable energy. While the Gainesville program was still active, the last of those laws, in state law in 2009, expired and had to be renewed.
But in the meantime, state governments had come to understand that FIT programs cost money, and they were reluctant to adopt them. In 2009, the federal government's stimulus bill included billions of dollars in grants and loan guarantees for renewable energy, but no new feed-in tariffs. A few years later, state laws in Florida and other states required utilities to buy more renewable energy, but not at any particular rate, and not from individuals. While Gainesville's program was still active, Florida, dominated by large investor-owned utilities, did not adopt the FIT model statewide.
Gainesville still has the largest municipal solar power capacity in the nation. That may be because it is a college town and because it's in north-central Florida, where the solar resource is good, but by some per-capita measures it was among the national leaders at the time. The city's program is still in place. It hasn't added any new capacity recently, and the rate has been cut to 18 cents per kilowatt-hour. But anyone who signed up in the early days of the program is still getting the higher rate, locked in for two decades.
In some respects, the Gainesville story has been a bright spot of recent history, proof that the United States could have adopted feed-in tariffs, if it had wanted to. In 2014, Gainesville's program added a modest amount to the average customer's monthly bill. But it was a time when natural gas was booming, and solar panels were still an oddity.
The story of the Gainesville feed-in tariff is also a reminder that state and local governments still have some power to shape energy policy. Under federal law, wholesale power rates fall largely under the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. But the Gainesville tariff was a retail rate, paid directly to homeowners and businesses, not to any power company, and that put it under the Florida Public Commission, which regulates retail rates.
The costs of the program were passed along to consumers, in the sense that they're part of the retail bill. But it's also worth noting that GRU at one point capped the new capacity at roughly 4 megawatts a year to control costs, and it was able to reduce the tariff for later participants, but the early contracts stayed locked in for two decades. If GRU had wanted to add more than 4 megawatts of solar, it could have raised prices for everyone, not just the people who signed up. In a different environment, it might have.
